entities.name: Eschiva of Saint-Omer
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Eschiva of Saint-Omer, a formidable noblewoman of the Latin East, held the title of Princess *suo jure* of the Principality of Galilee from 1240 to 1247, a rare instance of direct female rule within the Crusader states. Born into one of the most prominent families of Outremer, she was the daughter of Ralph of Saint-Omer, who had been titular Prince of Galilee, and Maria of Montbéliard. Her succession to the principality underscored the complex inheritance laws and the enduring influence of established Crusader lineages amidst the increasingly precarious political landscape of the mid-13th century.

Her brief reign was marked by the escalating internal and external pressures facing the Kingdom of Jerusalem. Eschiva inherited a principality whose capital, Tiberias, had already been lost to the Khwarazmians in 1244, following the disastrous Battle of La Forbie, a catastrophic defeat for the combined Crusader and Ayyubid forces. She married Odo of Montbéliard, a powerful and influential baron, around 1240, who subsequently acted as her co-ruler and regent. Together, they attempted to maintain control over the remnants of Galilee, a territory vital for the defense and economy of the shrinking Latin Kingdom, which was struggling against the resurgent Mamluks and various Muslim factions.

Eschiva's rule represents a period of significant fragmentation and decline for the Principality of Galilee. Though the title of Prince of Galilee continued to be claimed by her descendants, the effective territorial control of the principality had largely vanished after the Mamluk Sultan Baibars' campaigns in the 1260s. The formal dissolution of the Crusader states and the fall of Acre in 1291 rendered any remaining claims purely titular. Her legacy, therefore, is tied to the fading fortunes of the Crusader enterprise, illustrating the resilience of its nobility even as its territorial base eroded.
